headline: Kansas Gov.-elect Cindy Holscher backs legal cannabis after narrow win
dek: Holscher won Kansas by about 7,000 votes and says rescheduling eases the path; in Mississippi, Scott Colom unseated cannabis foe Cindy Hyde-Smith.
key_points: The Associated Press called the Kansas governor's race for Democrat Cindy Holscher on 12 November, nine days after the election; Republican Ty Masterson conceded.
Holscher supports legalizing cannabis and says federal rescheduling has softened some Republican lawmakers' views, but she faces a Republican-controlled legislature.
Kansas has no medical cannabis program; a 2021 House-passed medical bill died in the Senate Masterson led.
In Mississippi, Democrat Scott Colom defeated Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith, who signed a 2025 letter urging President Trump to keep marijuana in Schedule I.
body: Kansas will have a governor who wants to legalize cannabis. The Associated Press called the state's governor's race for Democratic state Sen. Cindy Holscher on 12 November, nine days after Election Day, and Republican Senate President Ty Masterson conceded about 15 minutes later, according to Kansas Public Radio. Holscher won by a little more than 7,000 votes, a margin of about 0.7 percentage points, Axios reported.

Holscher campaigned on legalization and has argued that the Trump administration's federal rescheduling move makes it easier to pass reform in Kansas, Marijuana Moment reported. A day earlier, a second late call removed one of the Senate's most consistent opponents of cannabis reform: Democrat Scott Colom defeated Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith in Mississippi.

Kansas sits between neighbours that sell cannabis legally, including Missouri and Oklahoma, yet it has never passed even a medical program. Holscher has leaned on that point. She told one interviewer that Kansas plates are already visible at dispensaries along the Missouri and Oklahoma borders, and that the state is losing the tax revenue and the safeguards that come with a regulated market.

She has put a figure on it. In a separate interview she said legalization in Missouri had produced $255 million in revenue, and that 65 to 75 percent of Kansans support legalization. MetaFlora could not check her Missouri figure against state data for this story, so treat it as her claim. Polling backs the direction of her argument: the annual Kansas Speaks survey from Fort Hays State University's Docking Institute found support for adult-use legalization at 58 percent to 21 percent, and for medical cannabis at 65 percent to 15 percent, with majorities across party lines.
> Kansas is the clearest test of whether federal rescheduling changes minds in a Republican statehouse, not just in Washington.

A governor cannot legalize cannabis alone. Holscher will face a Republican-controlled legislature, and the record there is long. The Kansas House passed a medical cannabis bill in 2021 that died in the Senate. The Senate Federal and State Affairs Committee held many hearings but voted in 2024 to table a limited medical pilot program, and an attempt to revive a medical bill on the Senate floor fell short. In 2024 a special legislative committee on medical marijuana declined to recommend legalization in 2025, saying lawmakers should first see how federal rescheduling played out.

That last point is now the opening Holscher is using. Rescheduling has happened, at least in part: an order effective in April moved state-licensed medical marijuana into Schedule III, and a DEA hearing is weighing a broader move. Holscher said before the election that the federal change has created a different attitude among some of her Republican colleagues, and that advocates are already working to educate members of both chambers. Outgoing Gov. Laura Kelly, also a Democrat, had already called on lawmakers to legalize medical cannabis.

Holscher also blamed Masterson, as Senate president, for blocking the medical bill in past sessions. Masterson's loss does not change the Republican majority in the legislature, so the first real signal will be whether Senate leaders let a medical bill reach the floor in 2027.
## The count is not quite final

Holscher's win is not official until the state certifies it. Counties must finish their audits by 16 November and then hold their official canvass; the State Board of Canvassers, which includes Gov. Kelly, meets on 1 December to certify the results, Axios reported. Because the margin was so close, state law required every county to hand-audit ballots from 10 percent of precincts.

Masterson could still request a recount, but Kansas only pays for one in a general election when the margin is within 0.5 points. Above that, the candidate must post a bond. A source close to Masterson told The Kansas City Star he does not plan to pay for a recount if the audit confirms the result, according to Kansas Public Radio's summary.
## Mississippi: a reform opponent leaves the Senate

In Mississippi, the AP called the Senate race for Colom on 11 November after absentee and provisional ballots were counted. He beat Hyde-Smith by fewer than 7,000 votes and becomes the first Democrat elected to the Senate from Mississippi since 1982 and the state's first Black senator since Reconstruction, NBC News reported.

Colom, a district attorney since 2016, has backed diversion programs and drug courts for nonviolent offenders, but did not address marijuana policy during the campaign, the Marijuana Policy Project noted, as reported by The Marijuana Herald. Hyde-Smith had a clearer record. In December 2025 she joined 21 other Republican senators in a letter urging President Trump to keep marijuana in Schedule I, and she opposed cannabis banking reform and Mississippi's 2020 medical cannabis ballot initiative. Mississippi later legalized medical cannabis by statute in 2022, and dispensary sales began in January 2023.

Colom's win gives Democrats at least 55 Senate seats in the next Congress, with Alaska still uncalled. That changes the math for banking and descheduling bills in 2027, though Republicans have picked cannabis opponents as their leaders in both chambers.

In Kansas, the audit deadline is 16 November and certification is 1 December. Holscher takes office in January, when the 2027 legislative session opens; watch whether she makes a medical cannabis bill a first-session priority, and how Senate leaders respond. In Washington, the new Congress meets in January with a larger Democratic Senate majority. Colom has not set out positions on rescheduling, descheduling or banking, so his first committee assignments and votes will be the first clear read.
